title: How to detect synthetic identity fraud
summary: A synthetic identity passes KYC because every piece of it checks out. What it usually lacks is the past a real person builds up without trying.
body_markdown:
The Federal Reserve's industry-recommended definition is the use of a combination of personally identifiable information to fabricate a person or entity in order to commit a dishonest act for personal or financial gain. In the US it usually means a real Social Security number, often a child's, attached to a name and date of birth that belong to nobody.


In identity theft, the criminal uses a real person's identity, and that person usually notices and complains. A synthetic identity's name belongs to nobody, so nobody watches the account. The real owner of the Social Security number is harmed, but is often a child who will not find out until they apply for credit or a job years later. That is why synthetic identities can build credit for years, and why the eventual loss is so often booked as an ordinary bad debt.


Most KYC checks ask whether the details on an application appear together in credit and data sources. After a synthetic identity has been applying for credit for a while, they do, because the fraudster's own applications put them there. A check that compares data against data cannot see an identity whose data was created for it.


The end of a synthetic identity's working life. After building credit, often for months or years, the fraudster draws down every available credit line and disappears. The Federal Reserve describes it as maxing out a line of credit with no intention to repay. Because the account paid on time until then, the loss often looks like an ordinary default.


Adding a synthetic identity as an authorised user on established accounts with long, clean histories, sometimes in return for a payment to the real account holder. The synthetic identity inherits the account's repayment history, which makes its own credit file look older and stronger than it is.


It helps with the most common version. The Social Security Administration's eCBSV service lets financial institutions check, with the customer's written consent, whether a name, date of birth and Social Security number match SSA's records, and it says which element does not match. That catches a real number under an invented name. SSA itself says the service does not verify a person's identity, and it only helps where a Social Security number is collected with consent.
